query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A two-step warm/cold deformation followed by a short-duration annealing that selectively recrystallizes the fcc lamellae while preserving the hard B2 phase will reduce boundary stress concentrations, thereby improving room-temperature ductility beyond 20% without compromising the high strength (≥1.5–1.8 GPa) of the as-cast eutectic HEA.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colonies (fcc + B2).
generation.intervention: Applying moderate warm or cold rolling to introduce high dislocation density in the fcc lamellae, followed by a short high-temperature annealing (~5–15 min at ~800 °C) to selectively recrystallize the softer fcc phase and maintain coherent interfaces in the hard B2 phase.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading. Rolling performed at moderate reduction levels (e.g., 30–50%), followed by controlled annealing under inert atmosphere to limit oxidation. Mechanical testing is performed at ambient temperature and quasi-static strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Partial recrystallization of the fcc lamellae refines grain boundaries while preserving the lamellar B2 framework, reducing dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: Locally softened and refined fcc lamellae accommodate plastic flow more effectively and impede crack initiation at boundaries, while the retained hard B2 lamellae maintain or even increase overall strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Tensile strength remains ≥1.5–1.8 GPa, with ductility (elongation to failure) increased to >20% at room temperature, outperforming the brittle as-cast alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA with a hierarchical lamellar microstructure typically demonstrates high strength (~1.5 GPa) but limited tensile ductility (~10%).
generation.boundary: Excessive annealing time or temperature may lead to grain/coarsening of both phases and reduce the strengthening effect. Under higher temperature service conditions, boundary coarsening could diminish the enhanced ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Exact annealing temperature and time needed to achieve the targeted partial recrystallization may vary with specific alloy compositions and rolling reductions, requiring careful process optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce multiple samples with identical rolling reductions but systematically vary the final annealing time and temperature. Compare microstructures and mechanical properties to those of the as-cast alloy.
measurements: Measure dislocation density and recrystallized grain size via TEM and EBSD.
Perform room-temperature tensile tests to quantify yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation.
Assess the interface coherency using HR-TEM to confirm the retention of B2 lamellae and partial recrystallization of the fcc lamellae.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the short annealing treatment does not result in significantly increased ductility (i.e., <15% elongation) or if it causes strength to drop below the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) established fine lamellar (fcc + B2) eutectic microstructures that combine high strength with moderate ductility. Subsequent studies refined these microstructures through cryo-rolling plus annealing (PMC5818523), ultrafine-grain engineering (PMC6353877), and precipitate-based strengthening (PMC6478865). Approaches exploiting hierarchical or dual heterogeneous structures (PMC6687781) improved strength-ductility synergy further, culminating in phase-selective recrystallization methods (PMC9365806) that attain ~2 GPa strength with >30% uniform elongation. Despite these successes, ductility can still be compromised by brittleness from dislocation pile-ups and microcracking near colony boundaries, indicating the need for more targeted boundary engineering to fully harness the ductility potential at room temperature.
decision.unsolved: Even with enhanced lamellar design and hierarchical structuring, local stress concentrations at internal boundaries can trigger early microcracking and catastrophic failure during tensile loading at ambient temperature. While partial and selective recrystallization remedies the issue to some extent, the precise control of interphase boundaries for optimal dislocation flow remains challenging. A cost- and time-efficient method to reproducibly refine and stabilize boundary structures has not been definitively demonstrated at scale.
decision.lever: A two-step warm/cold deformation followed by an optimized short-duration annealing that selectively recrystallizes the softer fcc phase while preserving coherent interfaces in the hard phase. The final microstructure would maintain a refined lamellar framework yet reduce boundary stress concentrations via local recrystallization of the fcc lamellae.
decision.why: Building on the effective strategies of cryo-rolling and annealing (PMC5818523) and the demonstrated success of phase-selective recrystallization (PMC9365806), this approach directly addresses dislocation pile-ups and microcracking by locally softening and refining the grain boundary regions while retaining lamellar strengthening phases to maintain or surpass the original alloy’s strength. Tensile strength is expected to remain at or above ~1.5–1.8 GPa, with ductility improved to >20% in room-temperature tensile tests. This outcome can be supported by measuring dislocation substructure and boundary characteristics via TEM and grain-orientation mapping. A falsification test could compare multiple annealing schedules (varying temperature/time) to confirm that only the selective-recrystallization condition drives the targeted microstructure changes and enhanced mechanical properties.
